artworks.title: Life in the village, 1627
artworks.description: When you encounter someone wearing historical clothing, they are playing the role of an actual inhabitant of Plymouth Colony. They will talk about historical events and lifeways as if they are happening in the present. You may tour the Village and enter about a dozen re-created buildings.
artworks.placeNote: Most visitors spend at least 2 hours.
artworks.galleryName: The 17th-Century English Village (the year is 1627)

artworks.title: Muster drill
artworks.description: You may be called upon to participate in a muster drill! Captain Miles Standish will teach you to follow his commands, and how the Pilgrims prepared themselves to keep their town safe.
artworks.galleryName: The 17th-Century English Village (the year is 1627)

artworks.title: Kitchen gardens
artworks.description: A goodwife might ask you to help her pound corn, visit the garden with her or help her make sage and salt toothpaste.
artworks.galleryName: The 17th-Century English Village (the year is 1627)

artworks.title: Pilgrim games
artworks.description: The Pilgrims worked very hard, but they had some time for recreation, especially activities that made them exercise their minds.
artworks.galleryName: The 17th-Century English Village (the year is 1627)

artworks.title: Nuhshwetu (house)
artworks.medium: Wampanoag house of saplings and bark
artworks.description: Step inside a wetu (house)! Take a seat on the soft fur-lined benches, warm yourself by the fire on cold days, and learn about home and family life of Wampanoag communities in the 17th century.
artworks.placeNote: The nuhshwetu has limited space: you may have to wait to go inside.
artworks.galleryName: Historic Patuxet Homesite on the Eel River: the nuhshwetu, the mishoon, the cooking arbor, the garden

artworks.title: Mishoon (dugout canoe)
artworks.description: Watch staff work on making a mishoon (dug-out canoe), using fire as a tool to shape the vessel. You may be asked to help by using shells to scrape the inside of the mishoon.
artworks.galleryName: Historic Patuxet Homesite on the Eel River: the nuhshwetu, the mishoon, the cooking arbor, the garden

artworks.title: Cooking area
artworks.description: At the cooking area, learn about the Wampanoag seasonal diet. Maybe something will even be cooking, like meat over the fire, or soup or tea over the hot coals.
artworks.galleryName: Historic Patuxet Homesite on the Eel River: the nuhshwetu, the mishoon, the cooking arbor, the garden

artworks.title: Garden of corn, beans and squash
artworks.description: You may see staff working in the garden, growing corn, squash, and beans. They will tell you about the seasonal work of growing food.
artworks.galleryName: Historic Patuxet Homesite on the Eel River: the nuhshwetu, the mishoon, the cooking arbor, the garden

artworks.title: We Gather Together: Thanksgiving, Gratitude, and the Making of an American Holiday
artworks.description: This exhibit focuses on the origins of one of America’s quintessential holidays. Plymouth/Patuxet is the place where the ancient traditions of gratitude in both the Indigenous and European cultures merged in the autumn of 1621, and a new holiday of gathering and giving thanks began.
artworks.placeNote: In the Visitor Center exhibit galleries
artworks.galleryName: Henry Hornblower II Visitor Center: tickets, orientation film, exhibitions, Plentiful Café, shops and restrooms

artworks.title: Painting the Past: The Marcia Sewall Illustrations
artworks.description: The artwork of Marcia Sewall, award-winning children’s book author and illustrator, from her three books inspired by the museum: The Pilgrims of Plimoth (1986), People of the Breaking Day (1990) and Thunder from the Clear Sky (1995). With hands-on activities and a reading nook for children.
artworks.placeNote: Davis Exhibition Gallery, Visitor Center
artworks.galleryName: Henry Hornblower II Visitor Center: tickets, orientation film, exhibitions, Plentiful Café, shops and restrooms

artworks.title: Along the Shores of Change
artworks.description: Your journey begins at the Visitor Center: after the brief orientation film, follow the pathways to the living history exhibits.
artworks.placeNote: Orientation theater, Visitor Center
artworks.galleryName: Henry Hornblower II Visitor Center: tickets, orientation film, exhibitions, Plentiful Café, shops and restrooms

artworks.title: Plimoth Cinema
artworks.description: The museum’s cinema shows independent and documentary films; see the website for what is playing.
artworks.placeNote: In the Visitor Center (separate tickets)
artworks.galleryName: Henry Hornblower II Visitor Center: tickets, orientation film, exhibitions, Plentiful Café, shops and restrooms

artworks.title: Humoral Gardens
artworks.description: Period medicinal gardens outside the Craft Center that demonstrate the Doctrine of the Humors.
artworks.galleryName: Humoral Gardens (17th-century medicinal plants)

artworks.title: The Fort-Meetinghouse
artworks.description: The colony’s fort, which was also its meetinghouse, at the top of the village street.
artworks.galleryName: The Fort-Meetinghouse at the top of the village street

artworks.title: William Bradford’s house
artworks.description: A re-creation of the house of William Bradford, governor of Plymouth Colony. The houses are furnished with reproductions of the kinds of objects the Pilgrims owned, with kitchen gardens behind them. When a role player is at home, they will talk to you as if it were 1627.
artworks.descriptionKind: Our note; the house names come from OpenStreetMap
artworks.placeNote: Not every house has someone at home: feel free to look inside.
artworks.galleryName: Bradford house

artworks.title: Threads of Identity: Wampanoag Clothing Across Generations
artworks.description: Clothing as communication and expression: among the Wampanoag, dress over the centuries speaks to a story of cultural resilience and adaptation. The exhibit features work curated and created by Indigenous staff and Native artisans from across the Northeast.
artworks.galleryName: Craft Center: potters at work, the Apothecary Exhibit, Threads of Identity · café, shop and restrooms

artworks.title: Potters at work
artworks.description: Inside the Craft Center you’ll see potters at work: skilled artisans create reproductions of historic items made in England and other parts of Europe during the 17th century, used in the English Village and sold in the shop.
artworks.galleryName: Craft Center: potters at work, the Apothecary Exhibit, Threads of Identity · café, shop and restrooms

artworks.title: Apothecary Exhibit
artworks.description: Learn about the Doctrine of the Humors, the prevailing medical theory in 17th-century England and Plymouth Colony.
artworks.galleryName: Craft Center: potters at work, the Apothecary Exhibit, Threads of Identity · café, shop and restrooms

artworks.title: Rare-breed animals
artworks.description: The English colonists relied on their farm animals for milk, meat and eggs. They probably brought goats, pigs and chickens on Mayflower in 1620; cows and sheep came a few years later. The museum keeps heritage breeds like them.
artworks.placeNote: Only service animals may come in, to protect the rare-breed animals.
artworks.galleryName: Nye Barn: the museum’s rare-breed animals

artworks.title: Dockside exhibit
artworks.description: Those unable to board can enjoy a close-up view of Mayflower from the dock, visit the dockside exhibit area, talk to modern crewmembers, and look at photographs of the interior of the ship.
artworks.galleryName: Dockside exhibit: photographs of the ship’s interior, talk with the crew (open to everyone)

artworks.title: Mayflower II
artworks.artist: Full-scale reproduction of the 1620 ship, built 1955–57
artworks.description: Plimoth’s full-scale reproduction of the tall ship that brought the Pilgrims to Plymouth in 1620. Built in Brixham, England, she arrived in Plymouth on June 13, 1957. About 25 feet wide and 106 feet long, with four masts and six sails; on the National Register of Historic Places since her restoration in 2020.
artworks.placeNote: Walk the main deck, the ’tween deck and the half deck. Not wheelchair accessible.
artworks.galleryName: Main deck (the waist): the masts, the capstan and the hatch down to the ’tween deck

artworks.title: The main deck
artworks.description: Talk with the crew and role players about the 1620 voyage and the ship’s working life.
artworks.galleryName: Main deck (the waist): the masts, the capstan and the hatch down to the ’tween deck

artworks.title: The ’tween deck
artworks.description: “I was immediately struck by how small the ship seemed, particularly in the ’tween decks, where the passengers were confined. How could 102 people, including three pregnant mothers, have survived more than ten weeks in a space this size?” (Nathaniel Philbrick)
artworks.placeNote: Down the large modern staircase from the main deck.
artworks.galleryName: ’Tween deck: where the 102 passengers lived for the voyage

artworks.title: Town Brook
artworks.description: A short, beautiful walk along Town Brook through Brewster Gardens leads to Plymouth’s waterfront, Plymouth Rock and Mayflower II.
artworks.placeNote: In spring you might see herring swimming upstream.
artworks.galleryName: Town Brook walk through Brewster Gardens to the waterfront, Plymouth Rock and Mayflower II

artworks.title: The millstones
artworks.medium: 54-inch bed and runner stones, 200 years old
artworks.description: On the grinding floor, the 54-inch bed and runner stones grind corn into finer and finer pieces. Most Saturday afternoons are grinding days: watch the miller turn out cornmeal and sampe (a northern form of grits).
artworks.galleryName: Grinding floor: the 54-inch millstones

artworks.title: Packing area
artworks.description: The millers fill real orders for grits, cornmeal and flour. Learn how the millstones grind different products, what can be cooked with them, and which local farms grow the grain.
artworks.galleryName: Packing area: what the stones make, and where the grains come from

artworks.title: The waterwheel
artworks.description: Water diverted from Town Brook turns the 14-foot diameter waterwheel that powers the mill. The mill reproduces the Plymouth colonists’ original 1636 grain mill on Town Brook.
artworks.galleryName: The 14-foot waterwheel, turned by water from Town Brook

artworks.title: The gears
artworks.description: Downstairs, come face to face with the mill’s gears: the massive face gear and the smaller wallower or lantern gear turn the vertical power of the waterwheel into the horizontal power that turns the runner stone.
artworks.galleryName: The gears: the great face gear and the wallower that turn the runner stone

artworks.title: Water power and river herring
artworks.description: Experiment with water power and simple machines, and learn about the river herring that swim past the mill in the spring to spawn.
artworks.galleryName: Hands-on exhibit: water power, simple machines and the river herring of Town Brook
